exercise.title: The dominant 7: the 5th chord with one more note
exercise.why: A chord is every other note of the scale stacked up, and a fourth note on the stack makes a 7th chord: on the 5th note of a major key that gives a major chord with a ♭7, the dominant 7.

cells.text:
The panel below shows the chord on every note of {{=key}} major, each with four notes: root, 3rd, 5th and 7th. Tap a chord to hear it.
{{chord:I}} is the 1st chord of the key, built on {{1}}, and {{chord:V}} is the 5th chord, built on {{5}}. With its 7th, the 5th chord is {{chord:V7}}: the only chord in the key with a major 3rd and a ♭7, the pair that makes a dominant 7.
Tap {{chord:V7}}, then {{chord:Imaj7}}, the 1st chord with its 7th. Practice until you hear {{chord:V7}} leaning towards the 1st chord.

Press Play below to start the backing track: {{chord:V}} for a bar, {{chord:V7}} for a bar, then two bars of {{chord:I}}. Say "seven" when you hear the note that joins the 5th chord in the second bar.
Practice until you hear the 7th arrive before the chord box lights.
{{?key}}In another key the chords are new, and the 7th still arrives in the second bar and leans to the 1st chord.
